extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and empirical investigators using induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for when and how inductive inferences and analogical arguments are justified, how far they may be extended in time and space, and how to treat hypotheses and the assumed law of causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative uniformities contingent on collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (sequences or coexistences of effects that are not ultimate laws of causation) are generally contingent on the particular collocations of primeval causes and are therefore more liable to be frustrated by counteracting causes than ultimate laws of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the collocation varies, a totally different set of derivative uniformities may result. Even when a derivative uniformity results from a combination of causes, the supervention of a cause capable of counteracting one of the conjoined causes will defeat the derivative law. Example: day and night are successive effects of causes (sun's light + earth's rotation); a change (rotation stopped, sun extinguished, second sun added) would falsify the derivative uniformity though not the underlying causal law. Such derivative uniformities are admissible only where collocations are known by experience (i.e., within observed conditions of time and place).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit extensions of empirical/derivative laws to adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical or derivative laws (not ultimate causal laws) can be extended beyond observed instances only to adjacent cases in time or space; confidence decreases the further one extrapolates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the warrant for expecting the sun to rise to-morrow rests on knowledge of the causes and their persistence; extrapolating to 20,000 years is far weaker because rare cumulative or new combinations of causes may arise over longer spans. Inductions authorize extension only to cases 'adjacent' (nearby in time/place/circumstance) to those observed; with greater distance into the future or across space, the probability becomes inappreciable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal knowledge to mere empirical generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the actual causes underlying a uniformity allows stronger and wider extension of the law than merely having an empirical conjunction of observed events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When causes are ascertained, we can judge whether known counteracting causes exist and thus have greater assurance when extending the law (both in time and space). Example: knowing the sun's light and Earth's rotation as causes gives more confidence about tomorrow's sunrise than a mere empirical record of repeated sunrises would. Knowledge of causes also lets us extend claims to the limits of the ascertained influence of those causes rather than merely to the local bounds of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical-law spatial extension requires same individual agents
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical law observed in one place can only be extended to other places if the new cases are presumably within the influence of the same individual agents (causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: discovering a new planet within the solar system that indicates connexion by revolving about the sun allows inference (with probability) that it revolves on its axis because known planets do so—this inference rests on the supposition of a common cause acting across the system. If the cause is unknown, extension across space is much more limited; when the cause is known, we may include the extreme boundaries of its ascertained influence in our extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy valid when resemblance concerns the material circumstance (fundamentum relationis)
rubrics_metrics.description: An analogical argument is as strong as it is demonstrable that the point of resemblance is the material circumstance (the fundamentum relationis) on which the inferred consequences depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the resemblance can be shown to be the relevant underlying relation (not merely superficial similarity), the argument may amount to a rigorous induction. Example (Whately/Ferguson type): calling a colonizing country a 'mother country' is analogical by resemblance of relations; if the relation invoked really determines the consequences, the inference is strong. Establishing that the shared relation materially determines the consequences converts analogy into conclusive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as inference from resemblance absent complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical reasoning infers that because B resembles A in one or more respects, a proposition true of A is likely true of B, but it falls short of a complete induction when no invariable conjunction between the resemblances and the inferred property has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula: two things resemble in some respects; a proposition m is true of one; therefore it is likely true of the other. This requires that the common properties are not known to be unconnected with m; if they are known unconnected, the analogy is invalid. Analogy supplies probability (not certainty) unless the resemblance is of ultimate properties that guarantee all derivative properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude properties known to be immaterial when reasoning by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: For analogous inference to be admissible, the properties common to A and B must not be properties already known to be unconnected with the attribute m being inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If by elimination or deduction it can be shown that certain shared properties have nothing to do with m, then those properties cannot support an analogical inference. The assumption for analogy must be that m depends on some property of A unknown to us, and B shares one or more of those unknown candidate properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for dissimilarities and conflicting analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Every dissimilarity proven between A and B furnishes a counter-probability to analogical inference; there may also be conflicting analogies pointing both for and against the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical strength is a competition between known agreements and known differences. Unknown properties are numerous and can swing the balance. Examples: amber shares some properties with vegetable and some with mineral products; a painting may resemble two different masters in different respects; a vase may resemble Grecian and Etruscan works—such conflicts undermine straightforward analogical inference. Where differences are among indispensable conditions for the inferred phenomenon, they may outweigh resemblances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of analogy scales with extent of ascertained resemblance and breadth of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical arguments approach the strength of induction when resemblance is very great, ascertained differences are very small, and our knowledge of the subject is extensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If after much observation B agrees with A in nine out of ten known properties, we may conclude with a probability approximating nine to one that B has a given derivative property of A. Analogical conclusions are most valuable for cases 'adjacent in circumstances'—i.e., when the new case closely matches the observed ones in relevant respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as a heuristic for experiment, not a substitute for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical considerations are most valuable for suggesting experiments and observations that may lead to positive inductions; hypotheses inspired by analogy should guide enquiry, not be treated as established truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even faint analogies can suggest useful experiments or 'experimenta crucis'; hypotheses that explain known facts and predict new ones are scientifically valuable for directing further tests. But one should not accept hypotheses as positive doctrine without the possibility of ultimate testing by induction; mistaking hypothesis for truth impedes discovery by narrowing inquiry to the fashionable theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive methods presuppose the universality of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: All the Inductive Methods rest on the assumption that every event (or beginning of every phenomenon) has some antecedent cause on the existence of which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Agreement and Method of Difference explicitly assume that a found antecedent is the cause because it is the only antecedent that can produce the effect in question; but this inference itself presupposes that every effect must have a cause. This is not proved by the methods themselves and requires independent justification; otherwise the reasoning is, in effect, begging the question (petitio principii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief or instinct is not epistemic evidence for causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that humans instinctively believe in universal causation does not constitute evidence for its truth; belief is not equivalent to proof and cannot substitute for evidence conformable to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological assertions that universality of causation is an 'instinct' or an unavoidable belief are insufficient for epistemic justification. Evidence must be that which the judgment-faculty ought to yield to—i.e., appeals to sense and consciousness and conformity to fact—rather than merely to what the mind happens to believe. One should appeal from judging faculty to faculties that take cognizance of fact.
